question: Italy is famous for pasta, but the area around Milan also became a landscape of which crop used in risotto?
note: Marshy land around Milan was converted to rice fields during the Renaissance. The city’s saffron risotto belongs to that local agricultural history as well as to restaurant menus.

question: The green sauce pesto gets much of its colour and aroma from which herb?
note: The traditional tools are a marble mortar and a wooden pestle. Alongside the leaves go pine nuts, garlic, olive oil and cheese; in Liguria, pasta with pesto can also include potatoes and green beans.

question: In the Neapolitan tradition of caffè sospeso, what does a customer pay for?
choices: Their coffee and one for someone else
A coffee to collect the following day
One coffee shared between two people
A coffee served after the café closes
note: The extra coffee waits for someone who cannot afford one. The customer and the eventual recipient do not need to meet: the café holds a small act of generosity between strangers.

question: What tool do experts use to listen to a wheel of Parmigiano Reggiano during inspection?
note: The wheel is tapped and judged by the sound it makes. Every wheel undergoes its selection inspection after twelve months of maturation, before it can receive the identifying selection mark.

question: Pizza was being sold in the United States before World War II. Who had carried the tradition across the Atlantic?
choices: Soldiers returning from World War II
American tourists after World War II
Restaurant chains expanding after World War II
note: Neapolitan migrants made pizza in American cities before its wider rise in popularity. A documented New York pizzeria was licensed in 1905, so the story cannot begin with soldiers returning in 1945.

question: In the famous story about pizza Margherita, whom does the name honour?
note: The story links the pizza to Queen Margherita’s visit to Naples in 1889. Historian Zachary Nowak has challenged the evidence for the episode, so it is best understood as a celebrated origin story rather than a settled account.

question: The shape of orecchiette pasta resembles which part of the body?
note: The name means “little ears”. This pasta is especially associated with Puglia, where a classic pairing is cime di rapa, or turnip greens, sometimes with salted anchovies.

question: Which city’s pizza-making craft is recognised by UNESCO as a living tradition?
note: The recognition concerns a living craft: preparing the dough, handling it and baking it in a wood-fired oven. Knowledge passes between generations of pizza makers, and the practice extends into family kitchens too.

question: Macchiato means “stained” or “marked”. What makes the mark in a caffè macchiato?
choices: A little milk in the espresso
A dusting of cinnamon on the cup
A drop of liqueur on the saucer
A spoonful of cocoa under the coffee
note: The name describes a small addition to the coffee. Hot or cold milk can be used, and cold milk may be served separately.

question: Bologna is nicknamed La Grassa, “the fat one”. What does this nickname celebrate?
note: Bologna’s other familiar nicknames point to different parts of its life. La Dotta refers to learning, while La Rossa refers to the city’s red appearance.

question: Rome feels like Italy’s inevitable capital. Which statement is true of the newly unified country?
choices: Its national parliament first met in other cities
Rome became the capital at unification
Rome and Florence shared the capital permanently
The capital moved between cities every year
note: Florence served as the national capital from 1865 to 1871. The parliament met in Palazzo Vecchio before moving to Rome.

question: Which Italian island is the largest in the Mediterranean?
note: Its history brings several Mediterranean worlds together. Greek colonies left their mark in places such as Syracuse, while Palermo’s Arab-Norman monuments reflect a different meeting of cultures.

question: After Vesuvius buried Pompeii, what did some survivors do?
choices: Moved into the intact forum permanently
Rebuilt the entire city within a year
Turned the buried streets into a museum
note: The eruption did not erase the city from memory overnight. Emperor Titus organised relief, and people returned to retrieve possessions from the disaster zone.

question: What is unusual about the traditional construction of Alberobello’s trulli?
choices: The stones are laid without mortar
The walls are made of baked mud
The roofs are woven from reeds
The houses rest on wooden stilts
note: These limestone buildings served as homes, shelters and storehouses. Their thick walls and conical roofs belong to a practical rural design that could also channel rainwater into cisterns.

question: What makes Matera’s historic Sassi neighbourhoods distinctive?
choices: Homes and churches cut into rock
Merchant houses with tall brick towers
Streets laid out in concentric circles
note: The settlement combines excavated caves with masonry built from the stone removed. Religious buildings are part of that same landscape: rock-cut churches and monasteries sit alongside dwellings.

question: The colourful villages of the Cinque Terre sit among stepped hillsides. What were those terraces made for?
choices: Drying fishing nets above the harbours
note: Generations built dry-stone terraces into the steep slopes. The famous coastal view is also a landscape shaped by agricultural work.

question: What covers the circular opening at the top of Rome’s Pantheon?
choices: Nothing; it is open to the sky
note: The opening, called the oculus, is about nine metres across. Rain really does enter through it, and drainage holes in the floor allow the water to escape.

question: Why did Venice order glassmakers to move their furnaces to Murano in 1291?
choices: To reduce the danger of fires
To keep the glass cool with sea breezes
To use sand found only on that island
To put workshops beside a new railway
note: Glassmaking required intense heat. Moving production to the island helped protect Venice while concentrating the craft in a place that became famous for it.

question: Why is Stromboli called the “lighthouse of the Mediterranean”?
choices: Its erupting material can glow over the sea
Its summit holds an enormous electric lamp
Its white cliffs reflect the Moon all night
Its harbour was the first to use a lighthouse
note: The nickname refers to the volcano’s frequent activity. Sailors could see the glow of erupting material from the surrounding sea.

question: In Venice, a traditional squero is a workshop for making and repairing what?
note: Domenico Tramontin learned the craft in the Casal family’s yard before founding his own in 1884. His changes to the gondola’s hull were so well received that other builders adopted them too.

question: Michelangelo’s David became a civic landmark, but where was it originally intended to stand?
note: The cathedral commission changed direction once the statue was completed. A committee chose a prominent position beside Palazzo Vecchio, giving it a different relationship with the city.

question: Leonardo’s The Last Supper was painted for which kind of room?
note: It occupies a wall at Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan. A scene of a shared meal stood in a room where the community itself ate.

question: In Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus, what does Venus stand on?
note: Despite its familiar title, the painting shows the goddess arriving at the shore after her birth. The pose draws on classical sculpture, while touches of gold give light to her long hair.

question: In Italo Calvino’s novel about Marco Polo and Kublai Khan, what does the traveller describe?
note: In Invisible Cities, each city has a woman’s name. Conversations between the traveller and the emperor connect the descriptions, turning an apparent travel account into a book about memory and how we understand places.

question: Why did Galileo’s observations of Jupiter’s moons challenge an Earth-centred picture of the heavens?
choices: They showed bodies orbiting another planet
They showed planets shining with their own light
They showed Jupiter was smaller than the Moon
They showed all orbits were perfect circles
note: In 1610 he observed four moons moving around Jupiter. The discovery did not settle every astronomical question, but it provided a visible counterexample to everything circling Earth.

question: Torricelli’s mercury experiment led to the barometer. What does that instrument measure?
note: Air pressing on mercury in a bowl supports a column in an inverted tube. The space above the column also gave scientists a way to study a vacuum.

question: Alessandro Volta stacked different metal discs with damp material between them. What had he made?
note: His device stacked alternating metal discs with damp material between them. Called a voltaic pile, it used copper, zinc and salt-water-soaked cardboard to produce electricity.

question: How did Pinocchio’s first readers encounter his adventures?
choices: In instalments in a children’s newspaper
As subtitles in a silent film
On cards sold with wooden toys
note: Carlo Collodi’s story appeared in Giornale per i bambini between 1881 and 1883. Readers originally followed the puppet’s life in separate episodes.

question: What helped the language of Florence become a model for standard Italian?
choices: Its adoption as the language of the Roman Church
Its use by the largest Italian merchant fleet
Its selection by the first national army
note: Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio gave fourteenth-century Florentine lasting literary authority. Later writers and scholars helped carry that Tuscan model beyond its home region.

question: Cremona’s instrument makers assemble more than seventy wooden parts into which instrument?
note: A handmade instrument in this tradition involves more than seventy wooden parts. Makers learn through training and apprenticeship, and their conversations with musicians help shape the finished sound.

question: The designer of the Vespa scooter brought experience from which field?
note: Corradino D’Ascanio drew on aircraft design, including landing-gear ideas for the front-wheel support. The scooter also made wheel changes easier and helped protect the rider’s clothes.

question: A horse loses its rider during Siena’s Palio. Can it still win for its neighbourhood?
choices: Yes, the horse can finish without the rider
No, it must return to collect the rider
Only if another rider takes the saddle
Only if every other horse is disqualified
note: The victory belongs to the horse’s contrada, or city district. The race lasts only three laps of the square, but the loyalties behind it are rooted in neighbourhood life.

question: In the Italian tradition of La Befana, where does the broom-riding visitor leave children’s sweets or coal?
note: Her visit falls on the night of 5–6 January, around Epiphany. It comes at the close of the Christmas season, after the presents associated with Christmas itself.

question: The projecting lower shape of a Venetian bauta mask helps its wearer do what?
choices: Eat and speak without removing it
See clearly through the side openings
Tie it securely beneath the chin
Fold it flat inside a pocket
note: The traditional disguise combined the mask with a cloak and a three-cornered hat. It concealed more than a face, allowing the wearer’s identity and social position to become harder to read.

question: The Moka coffee pot is an Italian design icon, but its name points to which place in the coffee trade?
note: Mocha was a Yemeni port associated with coffee. The pot’s name links an everyday Italian object to a trade route beyond Italy.

question: In the Italian card game scopa, whose name means “broom”, which action earns an extra point?
choices: Clearing all the cards from the table
Keeping all your cards until the end
Taking no cards during a round
Finishing with the most cards in hand
note: The name describes a sweep of the table. Scopa traditionally uses a forty-card pack, with three cards dealt to each player at a time.

question: The holiday name Ferragosto preserves a trace of which earlier world?
note: The word comes from feriae Augusti, the holidays of August. The celebration on 15 August also became associated with the Catholic feast of the Assumption.

question: What unexpected figures might appear beside traditional nativity characters in Naples’s craft shops?
note: San Gregorio Armeno’s makers add recognisable people from public life to the traditional scene. The craft can absorb the world outside the workshop.

question: Burano’s Lace Museum occupies a building once used for what?
choices: A school teaching the same craft
A royal residence for visiting monarchs
note: A lace school opened in 1872 to help revive the craft. The museum preserves the work in a place where making it was also taught.

question: The family game tombola, often played at Christmas, most closely resembles which game?
note: The Neapolitan game uses ninety numbers, traditionally drawn from a small basket called a panariello. Players mark the drawn numbers on their cards as the family waits for the next winning combination.

question: What helped Bicycle Thieves make ordinary life feel immediate on screen?
choices: Studio sets and established stage stars
Newsreel footage with a spoken commentary
note: Vittorio De Sica’s film follows a worker and his son looking for a stolen bicycle. Its approach became a landmark of Italian neorealism.

question: In Vivaldi’s Spring, a viola imitates a sound beside a sleeping goatherd. Which sound?
note: The Four Seasons comes with descriptive sonnets. Listening for the dog turns a familiar piece into a little scene with characters and sounds.

question: La Scala’s name survives from something that occupied the site before the opera house. What was it?
note: Santa Maria alla Scala stood on the site before the theatre. The opera house opened in 1778, carrying part of the earlier building’s name.

question: Why is the Giro d’Italia leader’s jersey pink?
choices: The organising newspaper was printed on pink paper
Pink was the national flag’s original colour
The first winner owned a pink bicycle
The colour represented the race’s highest mountain
note: La Gazzetta dello Sport gave the jersey its colour. Introduced in 1931, it carried a newspaper’s visual identity onto the road.

question: Italy’s flag is green, white and red. Why did its national football team adopt blue?
choices: It was associated with the ruling House of Savoy
It copied the colour of the first footballs
It was chosen to match the Mediterranean
It was required by the first World Cup rules
note: The team first wore blue in 1911, when Italy was a monarchy. The colour remained after the monarchy ended.

question: Before becoming Ferrari’s emblem, the prancing horse was painted on what?
note: It belonged to the Italian aviator Francesco Baracca, whose family encouraged Enzo Ferrari to use it for luck. Ferrari added a yellow background associated with Modena.

question: The famous theme of The Good, the Bad and the Ugly evokes which animal sound?
note: Ennio Morricone used a call-like motif and different timbres for the central characters. Flute, ocarina and voices helped build the western’s sound world.

question: In bocce, players throw larger balls towards a small target ball. What are they trying to achieve?
choices: Finish closer than the opponent’s nearest ball
Strike the target out of the playing area
Make every ball touch the boundary
Keep their own balls farthest from the target
note: The little target is called the pallino. A simple contest over distance can be played individually or in teams.

question: Italy’s Sanremo song festival helped inspire which international competition?
note: The televised festival offered a model for a song competition shared across borders. The first Eurovision contest followed in 1956 in Lugano, with seven countries taking part.

question: Early Monza combined a road circuit with which other kind of track?
note: The circuit opened in 1922 with routes crossing at different levels. Its original design helps explain its lasting association with speed.
